resident.chief_complaint: Progressive motor weakness and tingling sensation in both upper and lower extremities.
resident.history: Motor weakness initially manifested ten months prior and started in the lower extremities before involving the upper extremities. The patient also developed tingling sensation and numbness in both upper and lower extremities. Three months after symptom onset, she was evaluated at the neurosurgery department of another university for progressive motor weakness and tingling sensation. She was able to walk independently but with an observable mild wide-base gait. She reported weight loss of 10 kg during 2 months. CT and MRI showed OPLL at the level of C3-T1 and cervical spinal cord compression; on T2-weighted images, high signal intensity was seen in the cervical spinal cord at the C5-6 disc space level. Electrophysiological tests (NCS/EMG) were not performed at that time.
resident.physical_exam: Physical examination revealed mild motor weakness (Medical Research Council [MRC] grade 4+/5) in all extremities and mildly decreased tactile sensation in all extremities. Gait was independently ambulatory with an observable mild wide-base pattern. Reflex findings are not documented.

Weight loss of 10 kg over 2 months
OPLL at C3-T1 with cervical spinal cord compression on CT/MRI
High T2 signal intensity in cervical spinal cord at C5-6 disc space level

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord lesion (myelopathy), likely at C5-6 or multilevel due to C3-T1 OPLL. The pattern of progressive quadriparesis with sensory loss in all limbs and wide-based gait supports a cervical cord lesion, although upper motor neuron signs are not documented, so localization rests on an incomplete examination.

red_flags.finding: Weight loss of 10 kg over 2 months
red_flags.rationale: Unexplained by cervical cord compression; may indicate a systemic process (e.g., malignancy, metabolic) and warrants workup, but does not by itself provide an alternative explanation for the quadriparesis and sensory loss because the cord compression remains a plausible cause.
Absence of upper motor neuron signs (e.g., hyperreflexia, Babinski) prevents confirmation of myelopathy; this limits localization confidence but does not change the indication or plan.

Cannot exclude a coexisting peripheral neuropathy, which could contribute to symmetric weakness and sensory loss; this does not change current localization but should be considered if symptoms are atypical.

neurology.public_message: Localization is consistent with cervical myelopathy from C3-T1 OPLL, with T2 cord signal at C5-6. The clinical pattern—progressive quadriparesis with sensory loss in all limbs and wide-based gait—supports a cervical cord lesion, although upper motor neuron signs are not documented. Imaging-reported cord compression explains the dominant syndrome but not every finding. Red flags: (1) weight loss of 10 kg over 2 months—coexisting, unexplained by the cervical lesion and warrants systemic workup but does not currently offer an alternative cause; (2) reflex findings not documented—coexisting, limits confidence in myelopathic localization; (3) NCS/EMG not performed—coexisting, cannot exclude a peripheral neuropathy.

physiatrist_opening.public_message: This patient has mild myelopathy (MRC 4+/5, independent ambulation) from C3-T1 OPLL with T2 cord signal at C5-6. While progressive symptoms over 10 months and T2 signal change raise concern and argue against indefinite delay, a structured 3-6 month trial of conservative management remains a rational first step in the absence of clear upper motor neuron signs or rapid deterioration. Conservative care—including physical therapy, gait and balance training, posture modification, pain management, and close neurologic monitoring—has a reported success rate of about 50% for mild myelopathy, though outcomes are less predictable when cord signal change is present. I cannot overstate success beyond that. I strongly recommend completing the missing reflex examination and NCS/EMG before deciding surgery; weight loss also warrants systemic workup but does not preclude a conservative trial. Failure of conservative treatment should be declared only if any of my listed preconditions occur.

I already weighed the 10-month progression and T2 cord signal at C5-6 in my initial assessment and still judged a 3-6 month structured conservative trial to be reasonable given mild deficits (MRC 4+/5, independent ambulation) and absent upper motor neuron signs. I therefore hold my position: complete the missing examination and workup, but do not rush to surgery before allowing an adequate conservative trial with close monitoring.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 10-month progressive cervical myelopathy with imaging evidence of OPLL from C3 to T1 and cord compression with T2 hyperintensity at C5-6. The clinical picture of evolving quadriparesis, sensory disturbance, and gait ataxia is consistent with the reported cord lesion, though absence of reflex documentation and EMG/NCS leaves some localization uncertainty. The unexplained 10 kg weight loss requires systemic workup. Despite currently mild deficits, the combination of progressive symptoms over 10 months and cord signal change indicates a high risk of further, possibly irreversible, deterioration; conservative management alone would carry significant risk. However, major surgery should not proceed until missing evaluations are completed to confirm the diagnosis, exclude confounding peripheral neuropathy, stratify systemic risk, and secure the airway.
proposed_options: Urgent completion of diagnostic workup (full neurological exam with reflexes, EMG/NCS, systemic workup for weight loss, anaesthetic airway assessment) followed by surgical decompression, most likely posterior laminectomy/laminoplasty with fusion from C3 to T1, if no contraindications emerge.

A short, closely monitored conservative trial (e.g., 4-6 weeks) with physiotherapy and repeat clinical assessment, accepting a small risk of neurological deterioration; if any worsening occurs, proceed immediately to surgery.

Immediate surgical decompression without full workup, reserving systemic and electrodiagnostic evaluation for the postoperative period; this would expedite cord decompression but carries greater diagnostic and anaesthetic risk.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Urgent completion of diagnostic workup (full neurological exam with reflexes, EMG/NCS, systemic workup for weight loss, anaesthetic airway assessment) followed by surgical decompression, most likely posterior laminectomy/laminoplasty with fusion from C3 to T1, if no contraindications emerge.
disagreement_points: The physiatrist's recommendation of a 3-6 month conservative trial is not appropriate given the progressive course and T2 cord signal; this delay risks irreversible spinal cord injury.

The absence of reflex findings and EMG/NCS means that a peripheral neuropathy could be contributing to the limb symptoms, which may alter the urgency and expected benefit of surgery; rushing to surgery without these data is unsafe.

The unexplained 10 kg weight loss is a red flag that could indicate an underlying systemic disease affecting surgical risk and prognosis; it must be investigated in parallel but should not indefinitely delay decompression if myelopathy is confirmed.
deferred_questions_to_director: Decide whether to proceed with surgery now after urgent workup or accept a brief conservative trial as recommended by the physiatrist.
Confirm the surgical approach (posterior vs anterior) after reviewing the actual imaging, especially the K-line and extent of OPLL.
Approve the timeline for the urgent workup; I would suggest completing all essential evaluations within 1-2 weeks.
vice_opinions.public_message: After considering the imaging and clinical course, I believe this patient has progressive cervical myelopathy from OPLL that will likely require surgical decompression. However, before surgery we must complete the missing neurological exam, EMG/NCS, and systemic workup for the weight loss. I recommend urgent evaluation and a multidisciplinary decision within days, not months, to avoid irreversible cord damage.

director_rulings.final_decision: The department will complete urgent diagnostic workup before deciding between surgery and conservative management. This includes a full neurological examination with reflexes, NCS/EMG, systemic workup for weight loss, anaesthetic airway assessment, and formal imaging review with K-line measurement. Surgical decompression is likely indicated if myelopathy is confirmed and no contraindications are found; if workup reveals a significant peripheral neuropathy or systemic disease that better explains the symptoms, conservative management will be reconsidered. The department will reconvene within 1-2 weeks to review all results and finalize the plan.
